title: Midterm 1 review guide
lead: Every prompt on the Midterm 1 review deck, in order, with an answer written the way it could be said on the exam. Theme headings are turned into the question they ask you to answer, and a few predicted questions change one detail of a review prompt.

items.q: What is a phoneme, and how do we know which sounds are phonemes in a language?
items.a: A phoneme is the smallest phonetic unit in a language that can convey a distinction in meaning. We know two sounds are different phonemes when a minimal pair separates them, so swapping them changes meaning. Phonemes are not letters and not even specific sounds, because one phoneme can have several allophones.

items.q: How is the IPA consonant chart organized by features?
items.a: The chart is organized by place, manner and voicing. Place of articulation runs along the x-axis from the front to the back of the vocal tract. Manner runs down the y-axis by degree of closure, from closed to open. Voicing separates the members of each pair by whether voicing starts before, during or after the closure.

items.q: Compare /p/ and /b/ in terms of features.
items.a: /p/ and /b/ have the same manner and place, because both are bilabial plosives. They differ in voicing, which is the timing of phonation relative to the release of the closure. The same difference separates /t/ and /d/, so features make it possible to talk in general about the voiced stops /b/, /d/ and /g/.

items.q: How do we establish that a speaker really has two different low back vowels?
items.a: We have to find two words whose difference in meaning depends only on the difference between those vowels. That is a minimal pair, such as CAUGHT and COT for a speaker from the outer boroughs of New York City. If two phones are contrastive in a minimal pair, they are different phonemes.

items.q: How do minimal pairs show that English contrasts depend on a particular feature?
items.a: English has minimal pairs for /b/ and /p/, /t/ and /d/, and /k/ and /g/. In each pair, place and manner stay the same and only voicing differs. So these phonemic contrasts all depend on voicing, and this is known from comparing minimal pairs within English.

items.q: Why is it so important that phonemes are not letters?
items.a: Literate people easily imagine speech as an orderly stream of letter-like units, but it is nothing like that. A spectrogram of “A sore back is a real pain” is a continuously changing signal with no clean breaks between sounds. Neighboring sounds overlap, so phonemes are categories we identify, not separate pieces in the signal.

items.q: Explain Hockett’s (1955) Easter egg analogy.
items.a: Raw eggs of various sizes and colors ride a belt into a wringer that smashes them together. The eggs stand for the series of phonemes, and the mess stands for the speech signal. An inspector examines the mess and decides which eggs went in, and he represents the hearer. He only has to identify the eggs, not put them back together.

items.q: What are morphemes, and how do derivational and inflectional morphology use them?
items.a: Morphemes are the meaningful parts that words are built from. Derivational morphology combines them to create new words, such as recertification. Inflectional morphology changes the form of the same word to fit the sentence, such as knife and knives.

items.q: How is the word morphology derived, and what would we call a unit in text?
items.a: Morphology is morph-, from the Greek for form, plus -ology, the study of, which gives “the study of the forms of words.” The same process gives morpheme, just as phone gives phoneme. Following that pattern, a unit in text is a grapheme, built from graph-, the first part of graphology, plus -eme. The “oops” about graphology is a reminder that derived meanings are only partly predictable.

items.q: How does -hood show that derivation is productive but limited?
items.a: The suffix -hood means a state of being associated with the stem noun, as in brotherhood and sisterhood. It is not applied evenly, because each knight has his own knighthood while brothers share their brotherhood. Neighborhood uses -hood for a different job, and we say friendship rather than friendhood for no apparent reason.

items.q: Strong associates of “knife” can also be verbs. Are their meanings similar as verbs?
items.a: No, their verb meanings are not similar. To “dish it out,” to have “a forked tongue” and to “table the issue” mean very different things. So even zero derivation, which only changes the part of speech, does complicated and unpredictable things with meaning.

items.q: How can derivational morphology change the pronunciation of a word?
items.a: Adding affixes can change the phonology of the rest of the word. Certificate, certification and recertification move the stress and change vowels. Record and invite change mainly in stress between noun and verb. This is one reason for “The Chaos” of English spelling.

items.q: How does inflectional morphology change words, and why don’t we list inflected forms separately?
items.a: Inflection changes meaning in a predictable way, marking plural, third person singular present and past tense. Knife becomes knives, walk becomes walks and walked, and sing becomes sang. As Menn puts it, separate dictionary entries for singular and plural nouns would be silly. The sound change can still be irregular, as in mice.

items.q: How does inflection depend on syntax in a way derivation does not?
items.a: In the phrase “two [noun]+pl,” whatever noun goes there must be pluralized somehow, so syntax requires the inflection. No syntactic process requires even a very productive derivational form. A formula like “Once you [verb] it, you can un-[verb] it” is the closest case, but it is not exactly syntax.

items.q: What is activation, and how does it spread in a lexical network?
items.a: Activation is the graded level of activity of a node, such as a word, and it rises as evidence for that word grows. Nodes are linked by weighted connections set by association. So activating one word sends some activation to related words, which explains semantic and mediated priming.

items.q: How can words be represented in a simple lexical network?
items.a: Each word is a node, such as LION, TIGER and STRIPES, that can be activated by that specific word. The node must respond to the word in any case, font or size, which is a lack of invariance problem. Its activation level stands for how strongly the word is currently represented.

items.q: What does it mean that activation can be partial?
items.a: Activation can be partial when the evidence for a word is weak. When LION contrasts poorly with the noise mask, its node is only weakly activated. As the word becomes clearer, its activation increases.

items.q: What is the perceptual identification task, and how does the network model it?
items.a: In the perceptual identification task, participants push a button as soon as they can identify the item. In the network, this happens when the signal-to-noise ratio is very favorable and activity is strong enough to count as identifying “lion.” So response time tracks how quickly activation reaches that point.

items.q: How can activation dynamics explain frequency effects?
items.a: Experience tunes up a word’s activation dynamics, so words met more often are easier to activate. Each encounter might raise the word’s baseline level of activation, or strengthen its incoming connections so it activates more quickly. It might also change a threshold parameter, and each of these is a very simple form of learning.

items.q: Why does seeing a word again very shortly afterward lead to faster identification?
items.a: Activation does not rise and fall instantaneously, and it falls off more slowly than it rises. If the word appears again while activation is still high, its baseline is already higher than usual. So it reaches identification sooner, and this is repetition priming.

items.q: Why do neighborhood effects and related-word priming require adding something to the network?
items.a: Both involve one word changing the activity of a different word. Neighborhood effects depend on how similar a word is to other words. Associative, semantic or phonological priming depends on a related word seen just before. So the nodes must be connected for activation to pass between them.

items.q: How does spreading activation represent the associations measured in norms?
items.a: Connection strengths between nodes are determined by their association, as measured in the norms. When “lion” is activated, some of that activation travels along a weighted connection to “tiger.” So tiger is partly active before it appears, which is the spreading activation account of semantic priming.

items.q: What did Balota and Lorch test, and what did they find?
items.a: They tested whether activation spreads automatically beyond directly associated concepts, using pairs like lion and stripes linked only through tiger. In lexical decision, directly related pairs helped but mediated pairs did not. In pronunciation, both directly related and mediated pairs helped, so activation does spread beyond direct associates.

items.q: What is mediated priming?
items.a: Mediated priming is priming between two words that are not directly associated. Activity flows throughout the network, so activating “lion” spreads to “tiger” and then on to “stripes.” So lion can prime stripes through tiger.

items.q: Why is the Balota and Lorch result representative of psycholinguistics, and why would “stripes” prime “lion”?
items.a: It reflects careful study design and small effects, because the mediated benefit in pronunciation was only a little faster than neutral or unrelated primes. The result is counterintuitive, because stripes and lion are not directly associated. It happens because activation spreads through the shared neighbor tiger.

items.q: How can spreading activation lead to slower naming times?
items.a: A naïve view predicts that a block of similar pictures would speed naming. But related items spread activation to one another, so several competing lemmas are active at once. Selecting the right lemma from all the active ones takes longer, so naming slows.

items.q: Explain Lichtheim’s house model of aphasia.
items.a: Lichtheim’s house has a center for sound images (A), a center for concepts (B) and a center for movement images (M). An acoustic path brings sound in to A, and a motor path carries commands out from M. Specific aphasias come from damage to a center or a disconnection between centers. A break between A and B impairs understanding spoken words, and a break between A and M impairs verbatim repetition.

items.q: Describe Broca’s patient Tan.
items.a: In 1861, Broca presented “Tan,” who had lost the ability to speak after a brain injury decades earlier. Tan could only produce one jargon syllable. Otherwise he seemed to be in possession of his senses, and he seemed to understand what was said.

items.q: What did Tan’s brain show, and what was Hughlings Jackson’s criticism?
items.a: Tan’s brain had a large lesion definitely including the inferior frontal gyrus, the third convolution of the frontal lobe. This gave us Broca’s area, a part of the left frontal lobe important for speech. Hughlings Jackson (1874) objected that locating the damage that destroys speech and locating speech are two different things.

items.q: How did Lichtheim and Wernicke explain specific losses of language function?
items.a: They ascribed specific losses to disconnections between centers. A loss of understanding spoken words might come from a disconnection between A and B. A loss of verbatim repetition might come from a disconnection between A and M, and this center-based approach is an ancestor of modularity.

items.q: What was Freud’s holist critique, and what tension does it raise?
items.a: Freud criticized the diagram-drawing school as naïve for expecting the brain to be organized by psychological categories like word forms and concepts. He proposed that language emerged from fields connecting perceptual and motor abilities to drives. This raises the lasting question of whether brain areas map directly onto our descriptions of cognitive functions.

items.q: What did Dronkers and colleagues find in Leborgne’s brain?
items.a: Using MRI, they found the lesion was very deep and included the insula. There was also heavy white matter damage to the superior longitudinal fasciculus, which connects the front and back of the cortex. Other work by the group links speech apraxia, the condition Broca described, to the insula rather than Broca’s area.

items.q: What happens at the functional and positional levels of speech production?
items.a: At the functional level, the speaker selects lemmas and assigns them semantic roles such as Agent and Undergoer. At the positional level, a syntactic frame is built with slots for those lemmas and the particles the grammar needs. The slots also fix each word’s form, such as base form or past tense.

items.q: Why can’t we say we select “words” at the functional level?
items.a: The error “Where’d I bring it when I put it in,” meant as “Where’d I put it when I brought it in,” is the evidence. The verbs switched places, but the produced forms reflect a tense change applied later. This could not happen if “brought” had been selected, so the lemma BRING was selected and later expressed in the present form.

items.q: Why do people so often say the opposite of what they mean?
items.a: Antonyms are similar at many levels, being semantically related and strongly associated. They can also take the same semantic roles and belong to the same word class. So activation spreads easily from a lemma to its antonym, and the rest of the production system handles the wrong word smoothly.

items.q: How are lemmas slotted into semantic roles for “The plums in the icebox were eaten by me”?
items.a: The event structure is the same in the passive and in “I have eaten the plums in the icebox.” The verb is TO EAT, the Agent is ME, the Undergoer is PLUM and the icebox is the Location. Arranging these roles in a particular order, and turning ME into “I” or “me,” happens later at the positional level.

items.q: What has been accomplished by the end of the functional level?
items.a: By the end of the functional level, we have decided on a message to convey. We have selected appropriate lemmas and associated them with semantic roles. We are still nowhere near putting a clause together, much less saying it out loud.

items.q: For “Where’d I bring it when I put it in?”, what does the functional level supply, and what is left for the positional level?
items.a: The functional level supplies two verbs, PUT and BRING, with I/ME as the Agent and IT as the Undergoer of both. What is left is the temporal relationship between the verbs and the question structure. Expressing all of this syntactically is the job of the positional level.

items.q: What is in the positional frame for this sentence, and where does the error arise?
items.a: The frame is “Where’d I [verb, root form] it when I [verb, past] it in?” The first clause requires the base form, because of the question with an auxiliary verb, and the next clause requires the past form. The error arises while these slots are being filled with the lemmas from the functional level.

items.q: How is “a language needer learns” similar to the bring and put error, and how is it different?
items.a: It is similar because two lemmas got switched while being fed into the positional level, and the positional frame stayed mostly the same. It is different because the noun is actually a verb plus an affix. The derivational -er stayed in the noun slot and attached to NEED.

items.q: How is “He did that easy enoughly” similar to “a language needer learns,” and how is it different?
items.a: Both have a stranded affix, here -ly, which makes an adjective into an adverb. The difference is that something also went wrong while setting up the positional level itself. The adverb slot ended up second, so enough got the -ly and easy lost it.

items.q: What is stimulus control in experimental design, and why does it matter?
items.a: Stimulus control means choosing items that differ on the variable being tested but are matched on other properties that could affect responses. Without it, an effect can really come from a confounded variable. High-frequency words are generally shorter, so a frequency effect could be a length effect. Matching high- and low-frequency words for length rules this out, as Oldfield and Wingfield did.

items.q: What did Oldfield and Wingfield find, and what was the cautionary tale?
items.a: Oldfield and Wingfield (1965) asked people to name pictures of objects. They found a log-linear relationship, with more frequent names produced faster. The cautionary tale is that frequency is related to word length, even in a tiny sample, so the result was confounded.

items.q: What two patterns appear when the 200 most frequent words are put into ten bins?
items.a: First, mean frequency drops off very dramatically from the most frequent bin to the next, which is Zipf’s law in action. Second, length is inversely related to frequency. So the most frequent words are also the shortest.

items.q: What is the problem with selecting low-frequency words at random, and what is the solution?
items.a: High-frequency words are generally shorter than low-frequency words, so random low-frequency words will always be longer. The solution is not to select them at random. Picking longish high-frequency words and shortish low-frequency words matches length while still manipulating frequency.

items.q: What happened when Oldfield and Wingfield matched for length?
items.a: They still found a robust frequency effect. So they concluded that frequency effects are not merely length effects in disguise. Much of psycholinguistics is an attempt to show that an effect is not just an effect of some other confounding variable.

items.q: What is cyclic semantic blocking, and what causes it?
items.a: In cyclic semantic blocking, people repeatedly name sets of related or unrelated pictures, and related sets are named more slowly. Belke, Meyer and Damian (2005) found the effect only after the first cycle. Their controls and eye tracking place the cost at lemma selection, where related competitors slow the choice.

items.q: Summarize the three experiments of Belke, Meyer and Damian (2005).
items.a: Experiment 1 replicated semantic blocking and found it only after all objects in a set had been named once. Experiment 2 showed objects simultaneously and found blocking in naming latencies and gaze durations, but not in the gaze-to-speech lag. Experiment 3 found that blocking generalized to new, previously unnamed items. The authors proposed that the blocking effect comes from refractory behavior in the semantic system.

items.q: Why must we distinguish activation from selection, and how does WEAVER++ explain blocking?
items.a: Spreading activation from duck to fish means activating one helps activate the other. But the task is to select the correct lemma from many active ones. WEAVER++ assumes selection time depends on the ratio of the most active lemma’s activity to the total activation of all lemmas. Category feedback adds activation to every category member, so selection slows.

items.q: How do speech duration, gaze duration and lag map onto stages of production?
items.a: Speech duration fell over the experiment but showed no blocking effect, and it reflects the gesture level. Gaze duration showed a blocking effect after the first cycle, and it reflects lemma selection. Lag showed no significant effect, and it reflects phonological encoding, so blocking sits at lemma selection.

items.q: Does blocking generalize to new items in the same category?
items.a: Yes, the blocking effect generalized to new items introduced in cycle five. Overall naming slowed down dramatically and the repetition priming effect went away. But the blocking effect was still there, so it is not tied to repeating specific items.

items.q: How do Belke, Meyer and Damian isolate the blocking effect in the model?
items.a: It is not visual recognition, because the stimuli were normed and matched and a control experiment gave a different pattern. It is probably not phonological encoding, because the words are not phonologically similar and gaze duration, not lag, was affected. It is not just an effect of repeating lists, because it generalizes to new items.

items.q: Compare /t/ and /d/, and then /d/ and /g/, in terms of features.
items.a: The pair /t/ and /d/ shares place and manner and differs only in voicing, just like /p/ and /b/. Both /d/ and /g/ are voiced stops, so they share voicing and manner but differ in place of articulation. So any two of these stops can be described by which of the three features they share.

items.q: For a speaker who says CAUGHT and COT the same way, does that pair show two vowel phonemes?
items.a: No, for that speaker the pair does not show two vowel phonemes. A minimal pair only proves a contrast if the difference in sound changes meaning for that speaker. Most Americans outside the mid-Atlantic dialect say the two words alike, so they are homophones for them.

items.q: Is “knifed” an example of inflection or derivation, and how do you know?
items.a: “Knifed” has two layers. Zero derivation first turned the noun knife into a verb, and the past tense -ed is then inflection. The -ed is inflection because it adds predictable grammatical meaning to the same verb.

items.q: Would repetition priming be larger after a short or a long delay between the two presentations?
items.a: It would be larger after a short delay. Activation falls off gradually after the first exposure. So the sooner the word appears again, the more leftover activation it starts with, and the faster it is identified.

items.q: In Lichtheim’s house, what would damage to the pathway from B to M predict?
items.a: Damage between B and M would cut the route from concepts to movement images. So the person would have trouble turning ideas into speech. The path from A to M is spared, so verbatim repetition of heard words could still work.

items.q: Analyze the error “seat heaters” becoming “heat seaters.”
items.a: “Heat seaters” can be a stranded affix error, like “a language needer learns.” The stems seat and heat traded places, while the -ers ending stayed in the second slot. Because seat and heat differ only in their first consonant, it could also be a swap of those two sounds at phonological encoding. Either way, the ending stayed in its slot while the material before it moved.

items.q: Name another variable correlated with frequency that could confound a frequency effect, and how would you rule it out?
items.a: Age of acquisition is correlated with frequency, along with length, imageability and contextual diversity. Any of these could be the real cause of a frequency effect. To rule one out, choose high- and low-frequency words that are matched on it, just as Oldfield and Wingfield matched on length.

items.q: If semantic blocking had appeared in the eye-to-speech lag but not in gaze duration, what would that mean?
items.a: It would place the blocking effect at phonological encoding rather than lemma selection. Lag covers the time after the eyes leave an object, when phonological encoding and gesture planning continue. The real result was the opposite, which is why blocking is placed at lemma selection.
